Shopify Zendesk BigCommerce Klaviyo Magento Gorgias Salesforce Attentive Customers Back industries Apparel & Accessories Footwear Beauty & Skincare Healthcare Electronics & Gaming Home & Pets Food & Beverage See All Customer Stories featured Harry Rosen Achieves a 13-Point Conversion Increase with Narvar Resources Back resources Blog eBooks Reports Webinars See All Resources featured eBook The Claim & Effect Equation eBook The Return on Returns Company Back company Our Story Careers News & Press Sign In Request a demo EN English 日本語 Book a demo BLOG / CX Your SMS Program is Only as Big as Your Opt-in Published on: October 20, 2026 Updated on: October 20, 2026 5 min read By Narvar Team Your SMS and push programs reach only the shoppers who opted in. Ask at checkout and in My Account, and your delay alerts reach far more of them before peak. Key takeaways Your SMS and push reach is set by your opt-in list, and the list is set by when and where you ask. A tracking-page-only ask misses every shopper who never tracks, and it arrives after the first updates have already gone out. Checkout, My Account, and the tracking page each capture a different shopper. Order-level and customer-level opt-in let one yes cover more orders. Hibbett's notification opt-in rose from 20.5% to 35.8%. On 100,000 peak orders, that is 15,300 more orders reachable by text. Most enterprise retailers have already paid for the hard part of SMS and app push. The platform is contracted and the templates are approved. The carrier feed flags a late parcel before the shopper notices. Then peak arrives, a regional carrier backs up, and the delay alert goes out to a small slice of the people waiting on orders. The constraint is the list. A text reaches only the shoppers who said yes, and push reaches only the ones who allowed it. How many say yes comes down to when and where you ask. Ask late, and your program stays small however good the messages are. Ask while shoppers are already handing you their details, and the same program reaches a far larger audience before the first holiday order ships. Want the full shopper data behind these numbers? We asked 1,348 shoppers what they want from brands this holiday season. Download the report. . A tracking-page-only ask misses every shopper who never tracks Two enterprise retailers described the same setup to Narvar this year: the tracking page was the main place a shopper could sign up for text updates. That page should keep its opt-in. As the sole entry point, though, it screens out buyers before they ever see the ask. To reach a tracking page, a shopper needs a shipped order and a reason to click. One of those retailers told Narvar plainly that not every customer tracks a package, so its opt-in rate had a ceiling. The other said only a low share of its packages receive SMS updates, because most of its opt-ins come from the tracking page. The timing compounds the problem. By the time someone lands on the tracking page, the order confirmation and shipment notice are behind them. Any delay that surfaced early in fulfillment went out by email, or not at all. Delays are common at peak. In the 2026 Holiday Shopping Report from Narvar and eTail Insights, 37% of US shoppers said a package arrived late last peak, and 37% saw the delivery date change after purchase. That is where WISMO tickets come from. The shopper most likely to call you in December is the one whose parcel is late and who never heard about it. If that shopper never opted in, your delay alert has no number to go to, and the contact lands in your support queue. Three moments when shoppers are ready to say yes Shoppers agree to updates when the request fits what they are already doing. Three moments qualify, and each does a different job. Checkout is your highest-intent ask At checkout, the shopper is typing a phone number and watching the delivery date. A checkbox for text updates fits that task. With Narvar Notify , the checkout opt-in travels with the order data you already send Narvar through the Order API. It applies at the order level, so one yes covers every shipment in the order. It also covers in-store pickups, return shipments and pre-shipment updates for retailers that send them. On a split shipment, the second and third boxes get the same updates as the first. My Account turns one yes into a standing preference The account page is where shoppers set preferences they expect you to remember. Notify supports customer-level opt-in: a shopper agrees once, and the preference carries to future orders. Narvar's notification preference center embeds in My Account and on the order confirmation page. This is what enterprise teams mean by preference management. One retailer told Narvar its goal was to let customers opt in once at the profile level and never repeat it for each order. For a loyalty member who orders six times a year, that is six orders covered by one decision. The tracking page catches everyone else The tracking page stays in the mix because it reaches shoppers who skipped the earlier asks. Narvar's setup guidance for Track is direct: place the sign-up high on the page, and make SMS the default channel where it is enabled. A tracking-page sign-up also tries to subscribe the shopper to the full order before falling back to a single shipment. For retailers using Attentive or Vibes, the same sign-up collects consent for marketing texts in one step. If your checkout roadmap is full this quarter, start where the work is lighter. Move the tracking-page sign-up above the fold and add a sign-up prompt to the shipment, delay and delivery-anticipation emails you already send. Put the checkout field on the roadmap for the quarter after peak. What Hibbett's jump from 20.5% to 35.8% unlocks Hibbett Sports launched ecommerce in 2017 and built its post-purchase program on Narvar Track and Notify from day one. The goal came from the top of the digital team. "I really wanted to get past the 'buy' button and the order complete page." --Bill Quinn, VP of Digital Commerce, Hibbett Sports After Hibbett introduced its notification preference center, its notification opt-in rate rose from 20.5% to 35.8%, according to Narvar's Hibbett Sports customer story . The program went from reaching roughly one shopper in five to more than one in three. Hibbett also reported contacts per order down more than 20% after implementing Narvar. Put that rate change against your own peak volume. At 100,000 holiday orders, a 20.5% opt-in rate puts text updates on 20,500 orders. At 35.8%, the figure is 35,800. That is 15,300 more orders where a carrier delay reaches the shopper by text before the shopper reaches your agents. The shopper gains as much as the support team. In the same holiday report , 44% of US shoppers said order and delivery notifications would make them buy again. A bigger opt-in list means more shoppers...

blogs.content: Blog AfterShip vs Narvar: Which post-purchase platform fits your needs? Narvar vs AfterShip: compare tracking and returns, then see how parcelLab gives complex retailers more post-purchase control. { const isEventSignup = false; if (isEventSignup && window.dataLayer) { window.dataLayer.push({ event: 'event_cta_click', cta_location: 'hero', event_slug: 'aftership-vs-narvar', page_path: window.location.pathname }); } const matched = isEventSignup && typeof plab !== 'undefined' && plab.scrollToEventForm ? plab.scrollToEventForm() : null; if (matched === null && typeof plab !== 'undefined' && plab.scroll) { plab.scroll(document.querySelector('.Resource__Body'), -80); } })()" class="wp-block-button__link wp-element-button has-text-xs-font-size !py-3 !px-4"> Keep reading Back to Resource Hub published on October 19, 2026 = 1080 ? open = true : open = false;" @resize.window="window.outerWidth >= 1080 ? open = true : open = false;" class="w-full lg:w-[36%]"> Contents TL;DR: Short answer What is AfterShip What is Narvar What is parcelLab AfterShip vs Narvar vs parcelLab comparison: Choose the right post-purchase platform Narvar, AfterShip, parcelLab: When to pick which option Which should you choose for an elevated post-purchase experience? FAQs The Narvar vs AfterShip decision affects far more than package tracking. Returns can also expose serious margin loss. Appriss Retail’s 2026 benchmark puts the value of merchandise returned in 2025 at $706 billion. Fraud and abuse accounted for $100 billion in preventable losses. The two platforms promise to prevent such losses in different ways. AfterShip takes a modular approach centered on tracking and exchange-first returns. Narvar presents a connected suite led by IRIS intelligence and agentic automation. There’s also a third software option, however—one that offers more control across multiple markets and complex returns processes: parcelLab. It connects direct carrier data with customer communication and return decisions across markets. Let’s explore these three options in detail to help you choose the right post-purchase platform to keep customers coming back. TL;DR: Short answer AfterShip offers modular tracking and returns with public entry pricing. Its broad integration network suits ecommerce teams that want to select products separately. Narvar provides personalized delivery experiences, policy-aware automation, fraud prevention products and a physical returns network. parcelLab suits enterprise and upper-mid-market retailers managing several markets or demanding carrier mixes. It connects order-level tracking with branded communication and dynamic return rules. What is AfterShip Source: AfterShip AfterShip started as a standalone tracking tool and has since grown into a more complex post-purchase suite that connects with multiple popular carriers. The current version includes: Tracking: branded tracking pages with shipment notifications and carrier detection Returns: automated return workflows with exchanges and reverse- logistics tracking Shipping: multi-channel shipping and label management AI EDD: delivery date prediction for checkout and customer updates Warranty: warranty and claims management Order Edits: self-service changes before fulfillment There’s also a Channel Growth Suite for TikTok Shop catalog distribution and creator-led sales outside the standard post-purchase journey . Notifications and estimated delivery dates set clear expectations for shoppers on a branded page. The Returns feature set helps with revenue recovery with features like conditional workflows which check eligibility and route items, exchanges and store credit or partial refunds as alternatives to full refunds. Applicable plans detect serial returning and wardrobing. They can also flag policy abuse. Supported programs add printless QR returns and physical drop-off locations. AfterShip Agent assists with shipment exceptions, RMA review (US only), risk indicators in returns and approving suitable requests. It sends flagged cases to the retailer for a final decision. Published pricing makes initial comparison for predictive cost. Note that Tracking and Returns are paid add-ons. What is Narvar Source: Medium Narvar has grown from a single tracking tool into six products: Promise supplies pre-purchase delivery estimates. Secure offers delivery protection. Track provides personalized branded tracking. Notify sends proactive customer messages. Assist manages delivery claims and related fraud risk. Shield handles returns and exchanges, with return-fraud controls included. Narvar also includes an intelligence tool called IRIS. It uses retail data and behavioral signals to guide personalization and risk-based decisions. Shield can enforce eligibility, request extra verification or adjust refund timing. Retailers set different flows for products or customer segments. NAVI is Narvar’s customer agent which can answer delivery questions, show tracking information and offer policy-approved exchanges or trigger delivery-claim actions inside connected service platforms. Retailers define the rules governing those decisions. Narvar customers enjoy physical returns options, with printerless and boxless returns through carrier and retail locations. Availability depends on the market and selected program. Narvar offers custom pricing. See also: Narvar alternatives . What is parcelLab In an AfterShip vs Narvar comparison, parcelLab offers enterprise and upper-mid-market retailers a third option. It’s a user-friendly, fully customizable post-purchase experience platform for enterprise retailers and upper-mid-market companies that connects checkout promise with live shipment events and branded communication. Return decisions can use the same structured order and tracking data. The product has four modules: Convert: Promise calculates estimated delivery dates before checkout and can display them on product pages or during checkout. Engage: the branded Order Status Page and Messages & Journeys keep customers informed after purchase. Trending Late identifies shipments at risk of delay, giving your team time to notify customers before support tickets arrive. Retain: the self-service Returns Portal handles return requests and revenue-retention options. Fraud & Abuse Protection allows customer risk signals to shape return treatment. Insights: delivery reporting and communication analytics reveal operational problems. Returns data and benchmarking expose recurring reasons and patterns. parcelLab connects to over 450+ direct carrier API connections, including parcel carriers, freight providers and two-person delivery support. A common status model translates carrier events into consistent customer updates. Several tracking numbers are grouped under the original order so shoppers can follow every package on one branded tracking page. Your team sees an aggregated lifecycle state beside each shipment. The portal supports standard refunds and several revenue-retention options. Customers can make a direct exchange or switch to another product variant. Retailers can offer store credit and Shopify gift cards. You can also configure repair or warranty routes for eligible products. A retention offer can also let the customer keep the item they bought and get a partial refund. The returns process covers more complicated cases just as easily, with support for orderless returns, split returns and cross-border customs data. Fraud & Abuse Protection lets retailers adjust return treatment based on customer behavior for risk-based policies. When Fraud & Abuse Protection is enabled, a customer can receive a Fraud Risk Level of low, neutral, medium or high. Fraud Category records patterns like fast returns. You can use both fields as filters in the Returns Portal or across broader customer journeys. You can decide what each risk level changes, e.g., give a low-risk customer an instant refund and a 60-day return window, but reduce that window to 30 ...

blogs.title: 5 Boxing Day Marketing Ideas, with Examples from Real Brands
blogs.author: Tiff Regaudie
blogs.content: Personalized Boxing Day marketing strategies Generated by Klaviyo AI The article outlines five ways to reach post-Christmas shoppers using customer data, personalized offers, saved-product signals, and AI. It also explains how omnichannel messaging and automated customer service can support Boxing Day sales while collecting data for future campaigns. Sign up Get a demo Show AI generated summary For many consumers around the world, Christmas is the main event of the holiday shopping season. But Boxing Day on December 26 is the encore. According to data from MRI Software , in 2025, Boxing Day foot traffic was up 4.4% across all UK retail destinations, the strongest increase in 10 years. Though Boxing Day has British roots , the thrill of a good deal knows no borders. Today, people all around the world celebrate Boxing Day , primarily those in: The UK Ireland Australia New Zealand Canada South Africa Even if you’re a US-based brand, Boxing Day is a chance to reach shoppers in these markets and capture your share of their post-Christmas spend. Just make sure, if you’re using “Boxing Day” language and messaging (and you don’t necessarily have to), that you segment your audience by location before sending your Boxing Day marketing campaign. Here are 5 Boxing Day marketing ideas to help you close out the year strong: 1. Treat your VIPs to something special on Boxing Day Boxing Day is a good time to reward the customers who already showed up for you this holiday season. Tap into your customer data to see who's earned Boxing Day VIP treatment and what that should look like for them. For example, with predictive analytics , you could create a segment of VIPs with high predicted lifetime value. Or if you want to get more granular, recency, frequency, and monetary value (RFM) analysis can help you identify your most frequent buyers, biggest spenders, and most recent purchasers. That’s especially useful heading into Boxing Day, since a customer’s Christmas or Black Friday Cyber Monday (BFCM) activity is a fresh signal among your segments. Once you’ve found your Boxing Day VIPs, you can offer: Personalized premium picks for your highest spenders: Send an email, text or WhatsApp message, or push notification featuring what each VIP is most likely to buy next based on their purchase history. Give them a reason to add a little more to their cart with a free gift at each spending threshold. First dibs for repeat buyers: Launch a 24-hour early access sale that opens before your general Boxing Day sale. Bonus points for top loyalty tiers: Offer extra points on Boxing Day purchases, timed to nudge members toward their next reward before the year ends. Boxing Day marketing example: Sukoshi Mart gives VIPs early access K-beauty retailer Sukoshi Mart ties VIP treatment to app installs. In this Boxing Day marketing example, they give app users an hour of exclusive early access to sales, with a countdown timer to drive urgency. The email also turns Boxing Day into more than a single moment. Daily flash deals drop at noon every day December 19–31, giving shoppers a reason to come back daily rather than browsing once and leaving. Subject line: Boxing Day is HERE 🌟 Milled 2. Use customer data to rethink Boxing Day discounts Many brands default to discounts on Boxing Day, but they’re not the only way to win shoppers' attention. You’ll likely want to personalize incentives based on whether or not someone paid full price or bought at all before Christmas. Start with customers who shopped with you last Boxing Day, particularly those who bought from a product category you’re promoting again this year. You may want to determine your offer this year based on last year’s average order value (AOV). If shoppers spent around $50, for example, they might be willing to spend a little more if they get a free gift for spending $60. BFCM engagement can also indicate who’s still in the mood for deals. Customers who clicked or purchased from your BFCM messages and left positive reviews, for example, may not need a steep discount to purchase on Boxing Day. Those who purchased from a steep discount but didn’t leave a review may respond better to a stronger incentive, like a bigger discount or free shipping. An AI marketing agent can help you find relevant segments in your customer data and create targeted messages for each one. Here are some autonomous marketing prompts to try: Early access based on last year’s spend: “Build a segment of customers who bought from us last Boxing Day and have since bought from the same category. Use AOV within the segment to guide this year’s offer, which should surpass last year’s AOV as a spending threshold by about 10%. Create a Boxing Day email and text message giving this segment early access to this year’s sale, positioned as a perk for returning customers, with a free gift with purchase that matches this year’s target AOV.” Two offers based on BFCM reviews: "Segment customers who purchased during BFCM. Split them into those who left a positive product review and those who didn’t leave a review at all. For reviewers, create a Boxing Day email with a 10% discount. For non-reviewers, create a Boxing Day email with a stronger incentive, like a 40% discount, to bring them back.” Boxing Day marketing example: Dermalogica rewards high-value carts with tiered free gift offers In this Boxing Day marketing example, skincare brand Dermalogica gives shoppers a reason to spend a little more with tiered free gift offers tied to different order values. The offer rewards high-value carts without mentioning a discount. For shoppers comparing offers, getting something extra can feel like a better deal than paying less. Subject line: Your Boxing Day Exclusive Milled Boxing Day marketing tip: If you want to try something similar, ask your AI marketing agent to identify customers whose usual AOV sits just below one of your free gift thresholds. Then, ask your AI agent to draft a Boxing Day email and text message highlighting what they could get by adding a little more to their cart. 3. Create personalized mystery boxes based on browsing history Boxing Day has “box” right there in the name, so lean into it by creating personalized mystery boxes as product bundles built around what each subscriber has been browsing. AI product recommendations can help you decide what goes in each mystery box for each shopper. AI recommendations use a subscriber’s purchase and browsing history to choose products they’re likely to buy next. Then, rely on your customer data to decide how to reveal each mystery box offer. Channel affinity , for example, sends messages based on how each subscriber has interacted with your brand across email, text messaging , WhatsApp , etc., and ranks which channels are most likely to get their attention. Here are several ways a snack brand might approach this strategy on Boxing Day: Make WhatsApp part of the box-building process. Send a message with quick reply buttons asking, “Sweet or spicy?” Shoppers who choose sweet pick between chocolatey and fruity, while spicy shoppers choose between smoky and hot. Save their answers to their profile and combine them with past purchases to shape the final box. Use RCS to make the mystery box shoppable. Send a swipeable carousel of snacks that could make it into their box, with product images, prices, and tappable buttons for more details. Subscribers could tap between options such as “sweet,” “spicy,” or “savory” to narrow down what they’d like to receive. Send an email that gives subscribers a taste of what’s inside. Promise 6 full-size snacks in one personalized box, while keeping the exact selection a surprise. Link to a short quiz where shoppers’ answers and purchase history help determine the box’s exact contents. Follow up with a related offer on a different channel. If a shopper doesn’t engage with the first message, follow up on their second most preferred channel with a product clue, a partial reveal, or a last-chance...

blogs.name: Klaviyo Blog
blogs.title: How to Build Custom Klaviyo Product Feeds That Drive Conversions
blogs.author: Anna Sophie Fokdal Christensen
blogs.content: Build more relevant product feeds Generated by Klaviyo AI Custom product feeds combine Klaviyo’s AI-powered recommendations with catalog lookups and Django templates to control how products appear in emails. The approach supports richer imagery, dynamic pricing, additional catalog data, and reusable layouts across flows and campaigns. Personalized recommendations: Klaviyo uses browsing, click, and purchase behavior to rank products each subscriber is likely to want next. Flexible presentation: Catalog lookups and Django templates provide control over images, titles, prices, descriptions, vendor names, and variants. Dynamic merchandising: Custom logic can display sale details automatically and exclude out-of-stock, discontinued, or otherwise unsuitable products. Sign up Get a demo Show AI generated summary As head of email and retention at FABO , a holistic ecommerce growth partner for lifestyle and apparel brands, I spend a lot of my time inside brands’ product feeds . Most of them are showing customers less than they could be. First, a level-set: product feeds take in data from your product catalog and subscriber behavior (both purchasing and onsite behavior) and use this information to provide custom product recommendations for your subscribers. The approach I’ll walk you through both is and isn’t AI. The customization itself runs on Klaviyo’s catalog lookups and templating tools. But the data behind it, the part that decides which products actually show up for each person is Klaviyo's built-in AI . Put those two pieces together and you get product feeds that feel hand-built for every subscriber, without spending hours designing every email. Start with Klaviyo’s default product feed block Klaviyo’s default drag-and-drop product feed block is a solid foundation. You can choose how many products to show, where the button sits, and what the button says. For a lot of brands, that’s enough. But for lifestyle and apparel brands specifically, it usually isn’t. Klaviyo pulls the first image in a product’s photo array, and for most apparel brands, that first image is a plain product shot on a white background. The same brand usually has a full library of images showing that product on a model, in a real setting, and styled the way it’s meant to be worn. But none of that ends up in the default feed. The default block also places a hard ceiling on what you can customize. You can move elements around and change the copy on the button, but you can’t restyle the product name or price, or add another data point, like a brand name or a short description. If your merchandising needs anything more specific than that, you’ve hit the edge of what the default block can do. Send personalized product recommendations even if you don’t know your subscribers Here’s where the actual intelligence comes in. When you build a product feed in Klaviyo, you can pull from personalized product recommendations , a feature that uses AI to surface the items a specific person is most likely to want next, based on what they’ve browsed, clicked, and bought. This feature improves rapidly: what it recommends now is sharper than it was even a few months ago, and it’s the piece that makes personalization possible at scale. You don’t need to know anything about a brand-new subscriber to send them something relevant. Klaviyo already knows what they’ve looked at, and it can hand you a ranked list of what they’re likely to want next. That’s the data source. Everything else is about how you choose to display it. You don’t need to know anything about a brand-new subscriber to send them something relevant. How to build a custom product feed with catalog lookups and Django Instead of dropping in the standard block, I build my own tables using Klaviyo’s catalog lookups , paired with Django , the templating language behind them. It sounds more technical than it is: you’re calling specific catalog fields into an email template and formatting each one however you want, row by row. Once that’s set up, a few things become possible that you can’t do with the default block: You can choose which image shows. Instead of settling for whatever sits first in the array, you can call a specific image, like the on-model shot instead of the packshot, by referencing its position in your image list. You can build in your own pricing logic. A row can check whether a product has a compare-at price, then automatically show the original price with a strikethrough next to the sale price, or calculate and display the percentage saved. All of it updates on its own as prices change, so no one has to go back and edit each email by hand. You can pull in any other field your catalog has. “Vendor name” is one I use often for retailers that carry more than one brand, for example. “Description” works well for products that need more context. If it's in your catalog, you can include it. You can clean up messy product titles. If your product titles look like "Premium hoodie—ice blue / white," you can split that string and show the product name and the variant separately, styled however fits your template. You can control exactly what doesn’t show. That might mean out-of-stock items, discontinued products, or anything that doesn’t belong in front of a customer right now. You decide the rules. None of this requires anything Klaviyo doesn’t already offer. It's the same catalog and code structure available in every account. None of this requires anything Klaviyo doesn’t already offer. It’s the same catalog and code structure available in every account. Enrich your feed with a product catalog Sometimes, your product catalog data isn’t always formatted in a way that’s usable by a CRM, even though it already exists in your ecommerce platform. This happened with a jewelry brand I work with. Their Shopify catalog had rich data attached to every product: short quotes about the design, and a line or two on how each piece came together. But none of it was syncing into Klaviyo by default. I took the full Shopify catalog, ran it through a feed-management tool to shape the data the way I needed, and added it back into Klaviyo as a custom catalog . That let me pull those quotes and design notes straight into emails. It mattered here specifically because of the category. No one wants to scroll past 9 near-identical pieces of jewelry in the same price range and pick one. What actually works is fewer products, shown from different angles, on a person, with a little context about each piece. It’s a different set-up than a standard grid, and it starts with getting the right data into Klaviyo in the first place. Where a custom product feed fits in your flows and campaigns A custom product feed works anywhere a product feed does: welcome flows , retargeting flows like cart and browse abandonment , and email marketing campaigns . An apparel client of mine runs a win-back flow offering 10% off an evergreen archive collection. Because they sell across multiple currencies, a flat “on sale” message doesn’t always tell the full story. Instead, the button to the product calculates and displays the percentage saved for that specific product, in that specific currency, automatically. Another retailer client that carries dozens of different brands under one storefront needed customers to see which brand made the item they were looking at, not just the retailer's own name. Since vendor isn't something the default block shows, we built it into their custom feed instead. The common thread across every example is that showing the right image, the right price, and the right context matters as much as showing the right product. For another retailer client, unique conversions are up nearly 65% since we implemented custom product feeds into flows and revenue per recipient is up over 9%. Showing the right image, the right price, and the right context matters as much as showing the right product. If you’re already comfortable with catalog lookups and Django template filters, ...
